# FAQ: the hard questions

> Written to be honest about the state of the project. Every measured fact below is generated from
> the repository's own runs.

The measured facts quoted anywhere in `docs/launch/` come from the generated block below, which
`scripts/update_readme.py` keeps in step with real runs.

<!-- BEGIN facts -->
**Numbers you can quote** (generated by `scripts/update_readme.py` from real runs):

- Rules: 55 (26 CRITICAL/BLOCK, 21 HIGH/WARN, 8 report-only).
- 1195 tests run by default, plus 7 opt-in live-RPC tests that are skipped unless `TXWARDEN_LIVE_RPC` is set (the replay smoke test also needs `TXWARDEN_LIVE_REPLAY_CASES`).
- Synthetic labelled evals: 2660 cases in 92 categories; accuracy 0.977 (dev 0.977, held-out 0.976); BLOCK precision 0.988, recall 0.970.
- Disagreements with the labels: 14 unsafe ALLOW and 12 over-BLOCK, of which 0 and 0 outside the deliberately ambiguous `gray_area` group. Categories with any miss: `swap_impact_band`, `swap_loose`, `swap_mid_trade_slippage_band`, `swap_slippage_band`.
- The original 122-case set still scores 0.984.
- Prompt-injection eval (a scripted model that obeys every injected instruction): 245 runs, verdict weaker than the engine's in 0, changed after `assess_risk` in 0; 50 runs ended in a fail-closed BLOCK. No real language model was run.
- Not verified: any run against a real Ethereum node, real-world detection rates.
<!-- END facts -->

---

## How is this different from Rabby, Blowfish and the other wallet security checks?

It is much smaller, and I have not benchmarked it against any of them. As far as I know, those are
products: they are integrated into wallets, run against large proprietary datasets, carry threat
intelligence (known drainer addresses, phishing domains, token reputation) and have teams behind
them. TxWarden has none of that. It has no address feed and no UI, and it covers a fixed registry of
calldata, a few dozen decoded protocols' worth.

What it is instead: an **open, local, deterministic library** you can read end to end. Every verdict
traces to a named rule with documented thresholds you can change; nothing is sent to a third party;
the same input always gives the same answer; and it can be embedded (Python, CLI, or an MCP server
for agents). If you want protection for a daily-use wallet today, use a wallet that does this
properly. If you want a transparent building block, or to see how such a check can be made
tamper-proof against a language model, this is that.

## Where is the real-data validation?

There is none. Every evaluation number comes from **synthetic** cases whose labels I (the author)
wrote next to the rules, so near-perfect agreement is expected and says little about recall on real
attacks. What the synthetic evals are good for: regression (does a change move a verdict?), and
exposing threshold disagreements, which they did, in the open (README, "How well does it work").
What would count as validation: a labelled set of real transactions (drainer approvals, honeypot
buys, sandwiched swaps, benign DeFi interactions) scored blind. I do not have one. If you do and
can share it, that is the most valuable contribution there is.

## Is the "sandbox" realistic?

Partly, and the part that matters has not been tried against a real node. "Sandbox" here means a
dry run of the transaction (`eth_call`, `eth_estimateGas`, optionally `debug_traceCall` and
`eth_simulateV1`) against a JSON-RPC endpoint, typically a local Anvil fork. In this repository that
path is tested against an **in-memory fake chain** served over real HTTP, and against sessions
recorded from that fake chain. It has not been run against a real Anvil, Geth, Reth or Hardhat
node; response formats for reverts, call tracers and `eth_simulateV1` differ across clients and
are implemented from the specifications. An opt-in test file exists for you to run against your
node (`TXWARDEN_LIVE_RPC`); I could not run it.

Beyond that, a simulation is one block and one ordering. A contract can behave differently when it
detects a dry run, and state can change before your transaction lands. Those are in the threat
model as not covered.

## Why not let the model decide?

Because the model reads text the attacker controls: token names, revert reasons, calldata. The
verdict is therefore computed by code from the transaction, the simulation and your policy; the
model only explains. A test harness gives the agent a scripted model that **obeys every injected
instruction** and checks that the verdict never changes. That proves the architecture, not that a
real model resists injection: no real model was run.

## Does it need an API key?

No. The default is `--no-llm`-style deterministic output, and the explanation agent is an optional
extra. Tests and evals use a scripted model and need neither a key nor a network.

## What is the false-positive rate?

Unmeasured on real traffic. On the synthetic set the numbers are in the facts block above and in the
README, along with the categories where the engine disagrees with the labels. Expect warnings on
legitimate flows that touch unlabelled aggregators or vaults; the fix is to add them to your trust
lists, which is intended.

## What does it not cover?

See `docs/THREAT_MODEL.md`. The ones worth knowing before you rely on it: off-chain signature
requests (EIP-712), simulation-aware contracts, time-of-check/time-of-use changes, a lying RPC,
unknown protocols, and anything that needs history or threat intelligence.

## Can I use it as my only protection?

No. It is a second pair of eyes. Read what your wallet shows, use a hardware wallet, keep
allowances small, and revoke what you no longer use.

## Was AI used to build this?

Yes. An AI coding assistant wrote most of the code, tests and documentation in this repository (the
commits are co-authored in the git history). I directed the work. No real language model and no
live Ethereum node has been run against it yet, so the claims in the README are only the ones the
repository's own tests and synthetic evals substantiate; the rest is listed as unverified. Every
measured number is generated by a script, and the tests fail if the README drifts. The code is MIT
licensed and small enough to read; please do before trusting any verdict.

## Is it audited?

No.

## Why Python with no dependencies?

So it can be vendored, read and run anywhere without a build step, and so a security tool does
not bring a supply chain with it. The cost is a slow pure-Python Keccak (fine for selector tables)
and a hand-written ABI codec (tested against hand-assembled words and random round trips).

## How do I report a wrong verdict?

Open an issue with the transaction JSON and, if you can share it, the recorded session
(`txwarden review tx.json --rpc URL --record session.json`). A wrong ALLOW is the interesting kind.
